clue.text: Troublesome start while in very hot water?

definitions.meaning: surface reading: a difficult beginning to a new job or venture
setter's reading: a christening carried out not in cool water but in flames

explanation.walkthrough: 'In hot water' is the idiom for being in trouble; the setter takes it literally, picturing a christening by flames rather than by font water.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a first experience that is a severe ordeal, originally a soldier's first time under enemy guns.

clue.text: Snake that's savage squeezing a prisoner hard

indicators.note: to squeeze something is to hold it tightly between your arms, so one piece wraps around the rest

parts.note: a boor is a rough, uncivilised person
taken as written
con is short for convict
a hard regime is a strict one

explanation.surface: A vicious snake crushes a convict in its coils.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Squeezing' fits the snake perfectly, which hides that it is the container signal: the savage is split around the other three pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The boa constrictor is a large South American snake that kills prey by crushing it in its coils.

clue.text: Old Argentine leader wants agent gone after revolution?

indicators.note: a revolution turns something right round, so the letters come back in the opposite order

parts.note: with the agent gone there is no rep, a rep being a sales agent

explanation.surface: A former Argentine president, after a coup, wants rid of some spy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolution' looks like South American politics, but it is a turnaround; 'agent gone' is read as the phrase 'no rep'.
explanation.definitionFit: Juan Perón was the populist president of Argentina in the 1940s, 1950s and again briefly in the 1970s.

clue.text: A promise I broke around first of rules — fair boss?

indicators.note: to be placed around something is to surround it, so one piece goes inside the other
something broken is shattered into bits, so the letters are smashed and rearranged

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter, so only that letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone breaks their word about the rules and asks whether the boss is being fair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fair' reads as just, but here it is a funfair or show; the rearranged letters surround the single R.
explanation.definitionFit: An impresario organises and runs entertainments such as concerts, circuses or fairs, so is the showman in charge.

clue.text: A retreat under yours truly, most unpleasant

indicators.note: in a down clue, being under something means following it, so the pieces are joined in that order

parts.note: 'yours truly' is a jocular way of saying 'me'
taken as written
a nest is a snug hideaway

explanation.surface: Someone complains that a holiday hideaway lent to them was nasty.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'under' means the following pieces sit below, after the first one.
explanation.definitionFit: Mean in the sense of nasty or spiteful; the superlative matches 'most unpleasant'.

clue.text: Case of four, then twice that number for cargo

indicators.note: a case is the outside casing of something, so only the outer letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word
two times four

explanation.surface: A shipping order: a case of four bottles, then eight more as goods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' looks like a box of bottles; it takes the outside of the word, and 'that number' points back to four.
explanation.definitionFit: Freight is goods transported by ship, lorry or plane, a straightforward synonym for a load carried.

clue.text: North toured by first person from Berlin — not very far

indicators.note: a place toured by someone is one they travel all round, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: ich is German for 'I', the first person singular
N is the compass abbreviation

explanation.surface: A German traveller goes round the north but does not get far.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First person' is grammatical, the pronoun 'I', rendered in German because of Berlin.
explanation.definitionFit: An inch is a tiny length, so moving an inch is barely moving, as in 'not budging an inch'.

clue.text: Language one's pater translated

indicators.note: translating turns words into a different form, so these letters are reworked

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged; pater is Latin for father

explanation.surface: Someone's father's words have been put into another language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Translated' sits naturally beside 'Language', disguising that it is the signal to rearrange the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Esperanto is the artificial international tongue invented by Zamenhof in the 1880s.

clue.text: Feeling initially coming up in old cook for meaty dish

indicators.note: placed in something means put inside it, so those pieces sit within the other

parts.note: Mrs Beeton was the Victorian author of a famous household cookery book

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word
water welling up is rising to the surface

explanation.surface: An emotion wells up in a veteran chef as they make a hearty dish.
explanation.walkthrough: Isabella Beeton's 1861 Book of Household Management made her Britain's best-known cook; her name is split around the other pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Beef Wellington is a fillet of steak coated in pâté and baked in pastry, a classic main course.

clue.text: Hole, after reversing, crossed by a street vehicle

indicators.note: something crossed by another has it running through, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: a lane is a narrow road

indicators.note: reversing goes backwards, so the letters are read in the opposite order

parts.note: a pore is a tiny hole in the skin

explanation.surface: A car backing out of a pothole is hit by a vehicle crossing the street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hole' after reversing suggests a car backing out; it is the small hole turned round and set inside the street.
explanation.definitionFit: An aeroplane is a powered flying machine, a vehicle for air travel; 'vehicle' is a broad category.

clue.text: Area with trees where police heard?

indicators.note: something heard is taken by ear, so it is the sound rather than the spelling that counts

parts.note: cops is slang for police officers

explanation.surface: Somewhere in the woods the police are listening in.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for a small wood is pronounced exactly like the slang for police officers.
explanation.definitionFit: A copse is a small group of trees or thicket, a little wood.

clue.text: Lightweight knocked out on cue

indicators.note: something knocked out of shape is battered and disordered, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A lightweight boxer is knocked out right on time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lightweight' and 'knocked out' paint a boxing match, hiding the definition as a small unit of weight.
explanation.definitionFit: An ounce is a tiny imperial unit of mass, one sixteenth of a pound, so literally a light weight.

clue.text: Thus in power, government

indicators.note: something in a phrase is contained within it, so the letters lie inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: So it is with a government in power.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles the comma, ending one word and starting the next.
explanation.definitionFit: Ergo is Latin for 'therefore', used in English to introduce a logical conclusion.

clue.text: Financial gain, though lack of it for teacher

indicators.note: a lack of something means it is missing, so those letters are taken away

parts.note: profit is money gained
taken as written; these are the letters removed

explanation.surface: Money is made, though teachers notoriously see little of it.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface jokes about poor teachers' pay; the two letters of 'it' are removed from the word for gain.
explanation.definitionFit: Prof is the informal short form of professor, a university teacher.

clue.text: Lovely new party game

indicators.note: something new is made afresh, so these letters are reformed in a different order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
a ball is a formal dance party

explanation.surface: Someone praises a delightful new party game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party game' reads as one phrase, but 'party' belongs to the wordplay and only 'game' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Volleyball is a team sport in which a ball is hit over a high net by hand.

clue.text: Bond formed by boy in group

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece is placed within the other

parts.note: a set is a group of things or people
a boy's name

explanation.surface: A friendship is forged when a boy joins a gang.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bond' suggests friendship, or even 007, but is the noun for something that glues things together.
explanation.definitionFit: A sealant is a substance applied to bond surfaces or close gaps, a type of adhesive.

clue.text: Bonus drink after an assortment of Italian morsels

indicators.note: coming after means following in sequence, so the pieces are placed later in the line

parts.note: taken as written
a tip is an extra payment, a gratuity
Asti is an Italian sparkling wine

explanation.surface: After a platter of Italian nibbles, a complimentary drink is served.
explanation.walkthrough: 'An' is borrowed from the definition's phrase to lead the charade; the bonus and drink follow it.
explanation.definitionFit: Antipasti are Italian starters, a selection of cured meats, olives and vegetables served before the main meal.

clue.text: Clobber on, cuter after tailoring

indicators.note: tailoring cuts and reshapes cloth, so the letters are cut and reshaped into a new order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Clothes look cuter once put on after tailoring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clobber' is British slang for clothes, which fits tailoring, but here it is the verb meaning to beat soundly.
explanation.definitionFit: To clobber an opponent is to defeat them heavily, which is exactly what trouncing means.

clue.text: Taste of claret's in another drink

indicators.note: a taste is a small sample of something, so only part of the following words is used

parts.note: the letters run through the three words

explanation.surface: A hint of red wine turns up in a different beverage.
explanation.walkthrough: The run starts inside 'claret's', ignores the apostrophe, and ends at the start of 'another'.
explanation.definitionFit: Retsina is a Greek white wine flavoured with pine resin, so a kind of alcoholic beverage.

clue.text: Fruit with a soft cheese: no thanks!

indicators.note: saying no to something refuses it, so those letters are left out

parts.note: taken as written
p, piano, is the musical direction for soft
ricotta is a soft Italian cheese
ta is British informal for thanks; these letters are removed

explanation.surface: Someone offered fruit with soft cheese politely declines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A soft cheese' reads as one phrase, but 'soft' gives its own letter; 'no thanks' strips the final two letters of the cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: An apricot is a small orange stone fruit related to the peach and plum.

clue.text: Friend with limo adapted for biofuel

parts.note: a pal is a friend

indicators.note: something adapted is altered to suit, so these letters are changed into another order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A mate's limousine has been converted to run on green fuel.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a converted car, which happens to suit the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Palm oil, pressed from oil-palm fruit, is used as a feedstock for biodiesel, a renewable fuel.

clue.text: Stick on audio equipment for contentious argument

parts.note: a pole is a long stick
mic is short for microphone

explanation.surface: Someone fixes a microphone onto a boom for a heated debate.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, one piece placed on another sits above it, so the stick comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: A polemic is a strongly worded attack on or defence of an opinion, a fierce piece of controversy.

clue.text: Cloak, better back on vampire

parts.note: to cap a story is to better it

indicators.note: the back of a word is its rear end, so only its final letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A vampire's cloak is better worn on his back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back on vampire' suggests Dracula's cloak; it means the vampire's last letter, joined after the verb for outdo.
explanation.definitionFit: A cape is a sleeveless cloak worn over the shoulders, like the one Dracula famously wears.

clue.text: All leaders in opposition really antagonistic, Labour said

indicators.note: leaders are the ones at the front, so the opening letter of each word is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of each of the four words

explanation.surface: Labour claims every opposition leader is downright hostile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour' looks like the British party with 'said' as its verb, but it is the last source word and 'said' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Oral means spoken rather than written, as in an oral exam, so it is a synonym of said as an adjective.

clue.text: Country folk onto you

parts.note: ye is the archaic form of you
men are people

explanation.surface: Country people have found you out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country folk' reads as rural people; 'Country' defines alone, and the people are added onto the old word for you.
explanation.definitionFit: Yemen is a nation at the south-western tip of the Arabian Peninsula.

clue.text: Yowl! I am upset you trod on my paw!

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so these letters are tipped into a new order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
the cry of pain someone gives when trodden on

explanation.surface: A cat complains loudly after being stepped on.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the cat speaking; its pained exclamation supplies the final two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Miaow is the British spelling of the cry a cat makes, a yowl being a loud wailing cry.

clue.text: Minor irritation in dirty accommodation voiced?

indicators.note: something voiced is spoken, so it is how the word sounds that matters

parts.note: a pigsty is filthy living quarters

explanation.surface: A small annoyance about grubby lodgings is mentioned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minor irritation' suggests a nuisance, but it is literal: a small sore on the eyelid.
explanation.definitionFit: A stye is an inflamed swelling on the edge of the eyelid, a small infection that irritates the eye.

clue.text: Dawn has lit up place

parts.note: a light that is lit up is switched on
to place something is to set it down

explanation.surface: Daybreak has illuminated the town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dawn' looks like sunrise or a woman's name, but is used figuratively for a beginning.
explanation.definitionFit: The dawn of something is its beginning, as is its onset, e.g. the onset of winter.

clue.text: Go to pieces as top camera breaks

indicators.note: a thing that breaks shatters into fragments, so these letters are reassembled in a new order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A photographer falls apart when an expensive camera breaks.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like an emotional collapse, which suits the definition while the anagram does the work.
explanation.definitionFit: To go to pieces and to come apart both mean to disintegrate, literally or emotionally.

clue.text: One pocketed by foolish client, I'd want double!

indicators.note: something pocketed is tucked inside, so one piece is placed within the others
foolish means senseless, so these letters are thrown into a muddled order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A lawyer pocketing a fee from a gullible client demands twice as much.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Double' reads as asking twice the fee; it is the noun for a lookalike.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone's double is their exact lookalike, and an identical twin, from one split egg, is the ultimate one.
